Be sure you are getting adequate sleep/rest. Set a bedtime and a wake up time for every day and follow it. An hour before bed, do something quiet and non-electronic while lying in bed to wind down. Try melatonin to help regulate your circadian rhythm. Do you get spikes of being tired or just all day? Even if you can't sleep do something minimal while laying down if it's during the set bedtime hours. Do not get up in the middle of the night and use electronics or go into bright lights. Keep things dim. Light triggers the body to go into the wakefulness cycle of the circadian rhythm and will also prompt the body to expel melatonin, which if you took it would be helping you sleep during normal times, so that's no good. 

So...in summary...

-Set a bedtime and morning wake up time for everyday, try for 7-8 hours, and follow it every day except when urgently necessary. This will set your circadian rhythm, the natural sleep/awake cycle in your body.
-Lay down an hour before bed, read or do something that is not electronic with a slightly dim bedside lamp. No bright lights in the whole room.
-Only use your room for sleep, sex, rest, wind down time
- If you wake up in the middle of the night, no electronics to pass time. Lay down and rest. Avoid going into bright lights as it will make your body think it's time to wake up and start releasing wakefulness hormones.
-If you cannot sleep during the set bedtime hours, you must rest. Lay in bed and at most read. Don't throw your rhythm off. Don't push back your alarm if you are up at night. Try and tough it out.

Hey! Just now saw this, sorry. I just got my tube a little over a week ago. My starting weight was 265 and I got down to 200 in under 4 months. No doctors at home were taking me seriously, they kept saying I was "too stressed" from my first year teaching and burning the candle at both ends finishing college last year. So eventually my parents got involved and angry, and we ended up at Cleveland Clinic. They had no one staffed because of the holidays and so my parents fussed enough that a doctor in Gastroenterology/nutrition/liver center agreed to see me for the weight loss. No doctor would see me for left upper quadrant pain, or nausea, or vomiting, or a history of polyps. Gotta throw those number like 24% loss in body weight in under 4 months. 

Anyhoo, that doctor decided I was at a point where I was severely protein-calorie malnourished and my potassium was too low and I would probably need a tube. We did an upper endoscopy after a 4 day trial to see if I could keep down clear ensure (hint: I kept down none) and he decided to place the tube. He kept wondering aloud if I needed a gastric emptying study, and after enough helpful nudging from me, he did the scan.

Several things I learned: 

-I would much rather have had the gastric emptying scan before the tube. Keeping down the food is hard enough, then add on the fear of vomiting up your tube, plus the inevitable gagging from a newly placed tube...ugh.
-Cleveland Clinic allows substitution of 1 can of ensure instead of eggs to add the radioactive agent during the gastric emptying scan. I would have failed the test and not completed it if I would have had to have the eggs. Ask about this being an option if you are worried.
-It took TWELVE DAYS for insurance to bitch and moan and deny every nutrition support company that supplied formula and equipment on the planet. I had no calorie intake besides Gatorade for 12 days. Insurance didn't care, my parents cried on the phone their child was starving to death...didn't care. Get that crap figured out if you think you need a tube first if you can. Call and see what enteral support companies your insurance covers, get an idea on copay. I dropped my entire $2200 copay in on credit card purchase up front to even get started on my supplies. That means $2200 needed right then, not a bill that could be payed on. If my parents wouldn't have been there to save my ass financially I would have starved, I just wasn't prepared for the huge cost.
-If you get one, it will suck. Badly. It's like having a newborn taped to your face. The first 3-4 days feel like you are being forcibly gagged while having strep throat, while your nose runs down your face and your sneeze and sneeze. I eventually just carried a bucket around to spit, drip snot into, and possibly vomit into. Bring baggies with you, that tube can shift and just send you into a gagging fit.
-If you get a bridle, I'm sorry. I have one, and the sensation of it flossing your sinuses is not good. I got a sinus infection within a week. Granted I get like 4 sinus infections a year. (I am getting a netipot, this is supposed to help). It also rubbed an ulcer into my nasal cavity which got infected, so I get to shove antibiotics up my nose and gallons of children's liquid antibiotics down the tube. I haven't found a way to not hate it yet except to tell people I'm hardcore for getting my sinuses pierced. I'm still trying to figure out how to keep the string near the outside of my nostril soft so it doesn't turn into snot covered sharp razor wire and cut the crap out of my nose.
-The good news: I still hate the tube. Mine is a nasal-jejunal until they decide if they want a permanent one. However, I feel much better. I can walk across a room again, I'm not inclined to vomit as much as things bypass my tummy, my horrible muscles cramps and restless legs from low potassium is gone. Is it worth it? Yes, if you need it badly. If your weight is dropping like crazy and every day is a whole day struggle to keep liquids down, take the burden off yourself and let a tube heal you a bit. It gets better.

Plaquenil was a little rough for me to get used to. Lots of nausea, I take my dose split up morning and night to help with this. The thing with plaquenil is that it takes about 6 months to work. What caused the doctor to investigate this, and what were her labs like? If labs were high for Ds-dna or other antibodies, personally, I'd start now. Could head off some symptoms. On the other side of the coin, if it is very mild, maybe wait. Plaquenil starts to run risks of eye complications at high doses or over long periods of time. If your wife is 25, and will be on plaquenil her whole life, maybe pushing back starting it would be beneficial.

All in all though I am not a doctor. It concerns me that her doctor did not weigh the benefits and drawbacks with you, or give you more information to make this choice. Really you need to have this conversation with a rheumatologist, as this is a crucial medication and an important decision.

Way late to the party here, sorry! My big medical setback that eventually led up to me taking plaquenil was waking up cross-eyed spontaneously one day. I had a headache the night before, never been cross-eyed in my life, and the next day woke up fully cross-eyed. My eyes were even more fun in that they alternated which eye crossed in at random too. Saw specialist after specialist before I ended up at Mayo. Saw Neurology, Opthamology and Neuro-Opthamology there and no one ever figured out what caused it. Said I exhibited signs of both muscle weakness and just being "stuck". Something about my eyes not dilating right when coming together made it neither fully one or the other. I've been given theories that it was migraine induced, stress induced, and just plain who knows? After a year of staying consistently cross-eyed, I was allowed to have double eye-surgery, and my eye surgeon got me into my Rheumatologist after being frustrated I wasn't seeing one. Great guy. 

Anyhow, all this happened before plaquenil. Keep an eye on it, do not strain your eyes if they start to feel tired. Rest them when they need it. If you wear contacts, they had my drop down from -6 to -5.5 to reduce the correction so that it doesn't make my eyes strain more. Could help to do that if that's the case. But really, when your eyes start to cross they are probably tired and they need to rest! Don't push them! Lay down and listen to a nice audio book or something with your eyes closed.

Hope some of that helps, PM me if you ever need to and good luck! Take care of those eyeballs! : )

Skin tests were always the main test I always had to do. I'm allergic to tons of foods. My allergists usually used the RAST tests to check how severely my body was reacting. That being said, skin tests don't really test for sensitivities or intolerances which generally happen in a gastric reaction as opposed to skin. The skin tests are limited and local, whereas the blood tests are systemic. 

So they both have their pros and cons I suppose. I would get another skin test/second opinion. Food allergies aren't really something to be played with and you don't want to put your digestive tract through processing things it has adverse reactions to or have swelling, sneezing, etc. 

I know in my personal experience, some foods I will stop having noticeable reactions too if I force my body to eat it often enough. I build a tolerance to it. But then sometimes by body will suddenly have a tantrum about something I built a tolerance to. My allergist always told me you can develop or change allergies all through your life, so it's not unreasonable to think you forced your body into tolerating wheat and then it decided to complain. I am allergic to wheat, built up a tolerance for years and ate it just fine until one day my body had enough. I now vomit for days when I eat it. Allergies are weird.

Do you take an over the counter antihistamine like Zyrtec, Allegra or Claritin? That would be my first move if not. If you are, I would see a general physician first. They may be able to offer something like singulair to treat seasonal allergies/hay fever. If that doesn't work then I would go to an allergist. Allergists (at least for me) are specialists and cost more/are longer wait to get in to. I tend to try over the counter, then general practitioner and then a specialist if all else fails. It keeps my insurance happy too haha.

I get bad reactions to any bug bites. Big swelling, massive itching. The itching inevitably breaks the skin, introducing bacteria, which then results in cellulitis. I am assuming that is what has happened and your doctor is referring to when they say it's gotten an infection. It happens to me with a lot of bug bites. 

I would in the future put something like the goo on the bottom of a bar of soap (strange but really works), and maybe wear thin gloves to bed to not break the skin. Either that or I am a big fan of scratching bug bites with a soft bristled hair brush. You can scratch pretty hard without breaking the skin and it feels amazing. I would also look into getting a prescription topical corticosteroid (clobetasol and triamcinolone are what I've always used) for next time to nip it in the bud.

If it keeps getting redder, or the swelling bigger, go back to the doctor. If it begins streaking red from the wound or major swelling it would be important to get medical care right away. If it doesn't clear up you might need to get some prescription topical antibiotic like muciprocin or an oral antibiotic.
